paras.text: Michigan Legal System and Method, Audio Lecture

Welcome to the first chapter in the Michigan insurance law track. It is not about a single statute or a single case. It is the map you need before the other chapters make sense: which court hears an insurance case, which document beats which when two sources disagree, how to read a citation so you can find the real text yourself, what the Department of Insurance and Financial Services really is and is not, and the clock and boundary rules, statutes of limitations and unauthorized practice of law, that sit underneath every claim fight you will study later. Get it solid and everything after gets easier.

Let's start with the courts. Michigan splits its trial level jurisdiction mostly by dollar amount and by who the defendant is. The district court has exclusive jurisdiction over civil actions where the amount in controversy does not exceed twenty five thousand dollars. That number comes straight from M C L six hundred point eight three zero one. So a small water loss dispute, a few thousand dollars of contents, or a fight over a deductible often starts and ends in district court.

Once you cross that twenty five thousand dollar line, you are in circuit court, Michigan's court of general jurisdiction. The statute, M C L six hundred point six zero five, says circuit courts have original jurisdiction to hear and determine all civil claims and remedies, except where exclusive jurisdiction is given by the constitution or a statute to some other court. Most first party property insurance lawsuits, a homeowner suing a carrier over a denied or underpaid fire, water, or wind claim above twenty five thousand dollars, get filed here. Circuit court also shows up inside the appraisal process itself. If the two appraisers cannot agree on a neutral umpire within fifteen days, either side can ask a judge of the circuit court, in the county where the loss happened or where the property sits, to pick the umpire. That is written directly into the standard fire policy statute.

Now the court that trips people up: the Court of Claims. This statewide court, housed at the Court of Appeals, has exclusive jurisdiction over money, equitable, or declaratory claims against the State of Michigan or its departments and officers. That is the key phrase, against the state. Suing a private insurance company, State Farm, Auto Owners, a third party administrator, is not a claim against the state, so it belongs in circuit court. The Court of Claims only comes in if you are suing a state agency itself.

Above circuit court sits the Court of Appeals, the intermediate appellate court. It has jurisdiction as of right, meaning no permission needed, over final judgments and final orders from the circuit court, the Court of Claims, and the probate court. Some other orders, like an appeal from a guilty plea or certain interlocutory orders, are only reviewable if the Court of Appeals grants leave. Nearly every published Michigan insurance case you will study later, the ones setting the rules on policy interpretation, bad faith, and appraisal, came out of the Court of Appeals.

At the very top sits the Michigan Supreme Court, the court of last resort. It generally takes cases by leave, choosing which appeals to hear, and once it rules, that ruling binds every lower court in the state. Nickola versus M I C General, decided by the Supreme Court in May of twenty seventeen, is exactly that kind of case.

Put it together with an example. A homeowner's eighty thousand dollar fire claim gets denied. That is above the twenty five thousand dollar district court ceiling, so it starts in circuit court. If the insurer wins summary disposition and the homeowner appeals, the case goes to the Court of Appeals as a matter of right, because a circuit court final judgment is being appealed. Only if the Supreme Court agrees to grant leave does it go any further.

Now let's talk about precedent, published versus unpublished opinions. This is governed by Michigan Court Rule seven point two one five, subsection C. Here is the rule almost word for word: an unpublished opinion is not precedentially binding under the rule of stare decisis. Unpublished opinions should not be cited for propositions of law where published authority already exists, and a party who does cite one must explain why and how it is relevant. Compare that to a published opinion, which has precedential effect under stare decisis, and that effect does not go away just because someone asks the Supreme Court to review it.

In plain terms: unpublished does not mean useless or forbidden, it means not binding. A trial court can find an unpublished opinion persuasive and follow its reasoning, but it is equally free to reach a different conclusion. Tredenick, a twenty twenty one Court of Appeals decision from the adjuster licensing world, docket number three four nine eight eight seven, is exactly this kind of opinion: unpublished, persuasive only, never treated as settled law. Publication is not automatic either. The court rule lists eight standards, things like establishing a new rule of law, resolving a first impression question about a statute, or reversing existing law. If none apply, the opinion is deemed unpublished by default. To find the actual text of any opinion, published or not, or the current Michigan Court Rules themselves, go to courts dot michigan dot gov.

Next, the instrument hierarchy, ranking legal authority by how much force it carries. In Michigan insurance work you will hit four types constantly. At the top is a statute, an M C L section passed by the legislature and signed into law. That is primary, binding law, changing only if the legislature amends or repeals it. Below that is an administrative rule, one of the Michigan Administrative Code's R numbers, adopted by an agency like D I F S under delegated authority. It is binding, but subordinate to the statute that authorized it, and can be struck down if the agency exceeded that authority. A trap worth memorizing: rule five hundred point two two zero two sounds like a matching rule for siding or roofing, but it is actually titled discretionary clauses prohibited. Michigan has no matching statute or administrative rule at all.

Below an administrative rule sits a D I F S bulletin, interpretive guidance explaining how the department reads an existing statute or rule. It is not independent law, and the department can reissue or withdraw it any time, no legislative process required. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S, limiting labor depreciation on actual cash value payments, is a bulletin, not a statute, even though it has a real practical effect. At the very bottom sits a pending bill, with zero legal force until it passes both chambers and is signed. Senate Bill two forty five, proposing a first party bad faith cause of action, is a live example: reported favorably out of committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole, but not passed by either chamber and not law. Treat it as pending until that changes.

Now, reading citations, which saves enormous confusion later. Take M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision m. Five hundred is the chapter number, and chapter five hundred is the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, formally Act two eighteen of nineteen fifty six. Two eight three three is the section, the one in parentheses is subsection one, and the m is subdivision m. Read it out loud as act two eighteen of nineteen fifty six, section twenty eight thirty three, subsection one, subdivision m. The same logic works for chapter six hundred, the Revised Judicature Act of nineteen sixty one, Act two thirty six of nineteen sixty one, which governs Michigan's courts, jurisdiction, and civil procedure, including statutes of limitations and unauthorized practice of law.

Court rules follow a similar pattern. M C R two point one one six, subsection C, subsection ten, means rule two point one one six, chapter two being civil procedure, subrule C listing the grounds for summary disposition, and sub subrule ten the specific ground about no genuine issue of material fact. Case citations work differently: instead of a chapter and section, you get a volume and page in an official reporter. Four oh nine Mich four oh one means volume four hundred nine of the Michigan Reports, page four hundred one, and Mich with no App always signals a Supreme Court opinion, here Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance, decided in nineteen eighty. Compare two seventy six Mich App five fifty one. Mich App means the Michigan Appeals Reports, for Court of Appeals opinions, here Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance, decided in two thousand seven. An unpublished opinion never gets a reporter volume or page, so instead you cite it by docket number and decision date.

Let's talk about D I F S, the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, because people badly misunderstand what it can and cannot do. In its own words, D I F S provides consumer information, investigates consumer complaints, and works to assist consumers in resolving those complaints whenever possible. Notice that phrasing, assist in resolving whenever possible, and it encourages you to try resolving a dispute with the company directly first. When you file a complaint, D I F S investigates, and if it finds a licensed adjuster, solicitor, or insurance counselor violated the Insurance Code's licensing chapter, the director can order real consequences after a hearing: a cease and desist order, a civil fine, a refund of overcharges, restitution to the insured for losses caused by that violation, and suspension or revocation of the license.

But hold onto this boundary. D I F S cannot act as your personal attorney, cannot make a binding factual determination about who is right in a disputed coverage question, and does not order a private insurer to simply pay a claim the way a court judgment can. Even the restitution power is narrower than it sounds: it only reaches a licensee found, after a D I F S hearing, to have violated the licensing chapter. It is not D I F S stepping in as a judge to award general breach of contract or bad faith damages in a routine coverage fight. If a homeowner wants money out of an insurer, the tool is a lawsuit in circuit court, or appraisal where it applies. D I F S is the right tool for a licensing violation or a pattern of unfair practices, the wrong tool if what you want is a payment ordered.

Now, the basic shape of a civil lawsuit. It starts with a complaint, where the person suing states the facts, the legal claims, and what they want. The other side files an answer, admitting or denying each allegation and raising defenses, maybe a statute of limitations defense, maybe an exclusion argument. Then comes discovery: both sides exchange documents like the policy and claim file, send written interrogatories under rule two point three zero nine, and take depositions under rule two point three zero six, sworn out of court testimony. After discovery, either side can move for summary disposition, asking the judge to decide some or all of the case without a trial. The most common ground in insurance fights is M C R two point one one six, subsection C, subsection ten: except as to the amount of damages, there is no genuine issue as to any material fact, and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. In plain words, if the facts that matter are not really disputed and the law clearly points one way, the judge can end the case without a jury. If the case survives, it goes to trial, but a jury is not automatic. Under Michigan Court Rule two point five zero eight, a party must file a written jury demand, as a separate document, within twenty eight days after the answer, and pay the jury fee. Miss that window and the issues are tried by the judge alone, a bench trial.

Now the timing rules. Michigan's default statute of limitations for an ordinary breach of contract claim is six years, from M C L six hundred point five eight zero seven, subsection nine, the catch all for contract actions not described elsewhere in that section. A fire insurance policy does not get that six year window, because the standard fire policy statute writes its own, much shorter clock directly into the policy. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision q, requires suit within one year after the loss, or the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer. That phrase, whichever is longer, makes one year a floor, not a ceiling: a policy cannot shorten it below one year, but a longer contractual period would control. There is also a tolling rule built in: the clock pauses entirely from the moment the insured notifies the insurer until the insurer formally denies liability. Tolled just means paused, not running at all.

Here's the restoration claim example to lock this in. A pipe bursts in a basement on March first. The homeowner reports it that same day. The insurer investigates for four months and does not formally deny the claim until July first. Her one year clock did not run at all during those four months, tolled from notice until formal denial, so her effective filing window runs close to a full year from July first, not from the March first date of loss.

Last topic, unauthorized practice of law, and do not confuse these two statutes, because they solve different problems. M C L six hundred point nine one six is the general rule. It says a person shall not practice law, shall not lead others to believe they are authorized to practice law, and shall not call themselves an attorney, unless actually licensed to practice law in Michigan. The penalty is contempt of the supreme court and of the circuit court of the county where the violation happened, punishable as provided by law. The statute carves out one narrow exception: an attorney licensed in another state, temporarily in Michigan, handling one specific matter, does not violate it.

Separately, deep inside the insurance code, M C L five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a, exempts a person admitted to the practice of law in Michigan from needing a separate adjuster's license. That subsection lists exactly five exemptions: the attorney, a marine average adjuster, an insurer's own employee adjusting under the insurer's policy, a licensed producer with claim authority, and a supervised data entry clerk. These two statutes are not interchangeable. Six hundred point nine one six stops a non lawyer from practicing law or pretending to be a lawyer. Five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a, only tells you a lawyer who is already licensed does not also need a separate adjuster license. A contractor cannot borrow that exemption by working alongside, or being related to, an attorney. It belongs to the licensed attorney personally, and to no one else.

That is the whole map. Courts by dollar amount and defendant, precedent that depends on publication, an instrument hierarchy running from statute down to pending bill, citations that tell you where to look, a regulator that investigates but does not act as your lawyer or order payment, the basic stages of a lawsuit, and two very different one year and six year clocks. Carry this chapter into every one that follows.
